enrichment.short_title: Bankruptcy and standing to pursue unfair dismissal appeal
key_facts: Miss Grady, a prison service administration officer, brought employment tribunal claims for unfair dismissal, wrongful dismissal and disability discrimination after her employment ended in November 2000.
Her tribunal claims were struck out for non-compliance with directions and she appealed to the Employment Appeal Tribunal.
She was adjudged bankrupt in January 2002 before the EAT hearing; the respondent argued her appeal rights had vested in her trustee in bankruptcy.
The EAT dismissed the appeal for want of jurisdiction but granted permission to appeal to the Court of Appeal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal on whether a bankrupt employee retains standing to pursue an unfair dismissal appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed on standing; matter remitted to the Employment Appeal Tribunal for determination on the merits.
enrichment.ratio: A claim for unfair dismissal, including reinstatement or re-engagement, is personal to the employee and does not vest in the trustee in bankruptcy as a thing in action, unlike a claim for wrongful dismissal which is essentially a money claim.
legal_issues: Whether an unfair dismissal claim vests in a trustee in bankruptcy
Distinction between personal and proprietary causes of action on bankruptcy
Whether appeal standing differs from claim standing
Effect of hybrid claims containing both vested and non-vested remedies

enrichment.short_title: Homelessness review of suitable accommodation offer
key_facts: Ms Sharp sought to succeed to her mother's council tenancy at 63 Pharamond but Brent concluded she had lied about her residence period and obtained a possession order.
Accepted as homeless and in priority need, she was offered alternative accommodation at 29 Joules House under Part VII and Part VI allocation procedures.
She challenged the review decision that Joules House was suitable accommodation under section 204; the county court judge allowed her appeal.
The council appealed, arguing the judge confused succession, allocation and homelessness duties and misapplied Article 8.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Second appeal to the Court of Appeal under section 204 Housing Act 1996 from a county court decision on a homelessness review.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; the county court order was set aside.
enrichment.ratio: On a section 204 appeal the court reviews only the lawfulness of the council's decision whether offered accommodation was suitable under section 193; it may not re-open Part VI allocation choices or treat a refusal to allow the applicant to remain at her former home as the central issue.
legal_issues: Scope of section 204 statutory appeal on suitability of accommodation
Relationship between Part VI allocation and Part VII homelessness duties
Relevance of Article 8 where unlawful occupation preceded the offer
Whether dishonesty in a succession claim may inform suitability review

enrichment.short_title: Article 6 classification of customs restoration proceedings
key_facts: Traders and a vehicle owner appealed VAT and Duties Tribunal preliminary rulings on customs restoration decisions after excise goods were seized or detained.
Customs refused restoration under section 152(b), including a blanket non-restoration policy for revenue traders and a 25% payment requirement for an innocent vehicle owner.
The Tribunal certified preliminary points on whether the proceedings involved determination of a criminal charge under Article 6 and whether tribunal jurisdiction was Convention-compliant.
The Court of Appeal was asked also to rule on the meaning of seizure versus detention and on tribunal jurisdiction in forfeiture.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal on preliminary Article 6 and jurisdiction points from the VAT and Duties Tribunal.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed on the preliminary points; restoration proceedings held civil, not criminal, and tribunal jurisdiction adequate subject to stated concessions.
enrichment.ratio: Proceedings before the tribunal on a refusal to restore seized goods under section 152(b) determine civil rights and obligations rather than a criminal charge, and detention is distinct from seizure for appeal purposes under Schedule 5 to the Finance Act 1994.
legal_issues: Whether customs restoration proceedings involve a criminal charge under Article 6
Adequacy of VAT tribunal jurisdiction under Article 6 and Protocol 1
Distinction between seizure and detention under section 139 and Schedule 5
Whether the tribunal may re-open deemed condemnation without court proceedings

enrichment.short_title: Limitation on amending ACT compensation claim
key_facts: Hoechst UK sought compensation for timing disadvantage from advance corporation tax paid in July 1995 on a dividend to its German parent.
It had commenced proceedings in April 1995 listing earlier ACT payments but not the 1995 ACT, which was paid after issue of the writ.
Following the CJEC decision in Joined Cases C-397/98 and C-410/98, most ACT claims were settled but the 1995 ACT remained in dispute.
HUK applied to amend its pleadings to add the 1995 ACT claim after the limitation period had expired.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court application to amend pleadings in existing group litigation after expiry of limitation.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; existing pleadings did not include the 1995 ACT claim and amendment would add a new cause of action arising from different facts.
enrichment.ratio: Although the statement of claim referred generally to ACT paid since 1989, the quantified claim and schedule were limited to six specified payments and did not extend to the 1995 ACT; amending after limitation expired therefore added a new cause of action not arising from substantially the same facts.
legal_issues: Whether existing pleadings already covered the 1995 ACT payment
Whether amendment after limitation adds a new cause of action
Whether a new ACT payment gives rise to substantially the same facts as earlier payments
Effect of possible mistake-of-law limitation argument pending GLO test case

enrichment.short_title: Solicitor attendance at police disciplinary hearing
key_facts: William Melia, a pending armed robbery defendant and complainant in police disciplinary proceedings, sought permission for his solicitor to attend the hearing against two officers.
The officers allegedly supplied and permitted heroin use on his arrest; disciplinary proceedings were ordered to precede his criminal trial.
The presiding officer refused attendance because the accused officers withheld consent under regulation 26 and did not accept the solicitor as a friend under regulation 25.
The claimant argued refusal breached Articles 3 and 6 and would undermine fairness of his future criminal trial.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Expedited judicial review application for permission to challenge refusal to allow solicitor attendance at police disciplinary proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Application failed; no breach of Articles 3 or 6 established.
enrichment.ratio: Under the Police Conduct Regulations the presiding officer had no discretion to admit a solicitor without consent of all parties, and exclusion of the complainant's solicitor from disciplinary proceedings did not violate Article 3 or Article 6 given available transcript disclosure and separate criminal trial safeguards.
legal_issues: Construction of regulations 25 and 26 Police Conduct Regulations 1999
Whether a solicitor may attend as a friend or relative of the complainant
Engagement of Article 3 to police supply of drugs allegation
Whether absence of solicitor at disciplinary hearing affects fairness of later criminal trial

confidence.notes: Short expedited judgment with clear regulatory and Convention analysis.

enrichment.short_title: Judicial review of council nursing home fee refusal

statutes_considered.title: National Health Service and Community Care Act 1990

key_facts: Elderly dementia residents of Delamere House challenged St Helens Council's refusal to accept Southern Cross's proposed higher fees and block contract.
Southern Cross decided to close the home after the council rejected the terms; the council arranged alternative suitable accommodation nearby.
Residents argued the council decision was irrational and breached Articles 2, 3 and 8 because forced relocation would harm them.
No challenge was made to the suitability of the alternative homes; the dispute concerned the move itself and consultation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Substantive judicial review after renewed permission following refusal on the papers.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; council decision not impugnable on public law or human rights grounds.
enrichment.ratio: A local authority's commercial refusal to agree increased provider fees is not shown to have breached positive Convention obligations where Southern Cross chose closure, suitable alternative accommodation was arranged, and planned moves mitigated relocation risk.
legal_issues: Amenability to judicial review of contract negotiation with a private care provider
Positive obligations under Articles 2, 3 and 8 on relocation of vulnerable residents
Irrationality and failure to consider relocation risk evidence
Whether consultation requirements were satisfied

enrichment.short_title: VAT exemption for outsourced bank lending services
key_facts: EDS supplied outsourced customer lending and insurance services to Lloyds TSB under a 1999 master services agreement.
Direct supply by the bank would have been VAT exempt; the dispute was whether EDS's supply to the bank was similarly exempt under Article 13B.
The VAT tribunal allowed EDS's appeal against Customs' refusal of exemption and certified a point of Community law.
Customs appealed to the Court of Appeal contending the supply was standard-rated administrative outsourcing.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Direct appeal to the Court of Appeal from the VAT and Duties Tribunal on construction of Article 13B exemption.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; tribunal decision upheld and supply held exempt as transactions concerning payments and transfers.
enrichment.ratio: The integrated package of outsourced lending services formed a distinct whole whose core function involved payments and transfers changing the legal and financial position of the parties, so it fell within Article 13B(d)(3) as exempt transactions concerning payments and transfers.
legal_issues: Construction of Article 13B(d)(3) exemption for payment and transfer transactions
Whether outsourced bank services constitute negotiation of credit
Whether supply constitutes granting of credit under Article 13B(d)(1)
Single versus multiple supply analysis for VAT exemption

enrichment.short_title: Holiday pay under Working Time Regulations
key_facts: Andy Walker, a CIS insurance agent paid basic salary plus commission and procuration fees, complained his holiday pay did not reflect average weekly remuneration.
CIS continued its fortnightly payment system during leave, treating commission on a rolling annualised basis.
The employment tribunal held section 224 did not apply and dismissed the claim; the EAT upheld dismissal on set-off under regulation 16(5).
Applying the section 224 formula showed contractual holiday pay slightly exceeded the statutory calculation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal from the Employment Appeal Tribunal on Working Time Regulations holiday pay calculation.
enrichment.ratio: For a worker with no normal working hours, regulation 16 requires holiday pay by reference to section 224 average weekly remuneration, but contractual remuneration paid during leave may discharge the employer's liability under regulation 16(5) where it equals or exceeds the statutory figure.
legal_issues: Application of section 224 to commission-based insurance agents
Set-off of contractual remuneration under regulation 16(5)
Whether manual premium collections during leave create underpayment
Adequacy of written particulars of holiday pay under section 1

confidence.notes: Clear EAT and Court of Appeal analysis of WTR regulation 16 and section 224 with quantified findings.

enrichment.short_title: Setting aside default judgment for lack of jurisdiction
key_facts: Cargo interests obtained default judgment against Italian shipowners in a 1998 damage-to-cargo claim after service in Italy based on an incorrect jurisdiction certificate.
The bill of lading incorporated a contract of affreightment with English law and London arbitration, but general incorporation did not confer English jurisdiction on the owners.
Claimants obtained judgment without notice after an informal moratorium on proceedings while settlement talks continued.
Owners applied to set aside the judgment and challenge jurisdiction; the contractual time bar had expired in Italy.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application to set aside default judgment and declare lack of jurisdiction under the Brussels Convention.
enrichment.outcome: Default judgment set aside; proceedings dismissed for lack of jurisdiction; no estoppel against time bar defence.
enrichment.ratio: An incorrect certificate under the Civil Jurisdiction and Judgments Act 1982 cannot found jurisdiction over Italian-domiciled defendants where no Brussels Convention head applies, and silence during settlement discussions does not make it unconscionable to rely on an accrued time bar.
legal_issues: Validity of service based on incorrect jurisdiction certificate
Whether English law clause implies High Court jurisdiction
Setting aside default judgment obtained without notice
Estoppel by silence and duty to speak on limitation extension

enrichment.short_title: NASS dispersal and Article 3 protection for asylum seekers
key_facts: A Kurdish Turkish asylum-seeking family was dispersed by NASS to deck-access housing on the Toryglen Estate in Glasgow in September 2001.
They suffered sustained racial abuse and violence, including a knife attack in October 2001, and returned to London without support.
NASS initially required their return to Glasgow and withdrew support before later withdrawing the return decision.
The claimant sought judicial review and damages, arguing dispersal breached Articles 3 and 8 and section 95 accommodation duties.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of NASS dispersal and subsequent support decisions with damages claim.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; no breach of Articles 3 or 8 established, though obiter damages figure of £5,000 was indicated had liability been found.
enrichment.ratio: Before the October 2001 attack police had not advised that deck-access accommodation on Toryglen was unsuitable for asylum seekers, so NASS's general dispersal policy combined with police protection and support measures provided reasonably available Article 3 protection.
legal_issues: Positive obligations under Article 3 to protect asylum seekers from third-party racial violence
Whether NASS knew or ought to have known of specific risk on Toryglen deck-access housing
Adequacy of accommodation under section 95 Immigration and Asylum Act 1999
Entitlement to damages for Convention breach
